business.title: A system-based abstraction hierarchy framework for seismic risk assessment of urban transportation networks
business.desc: Urban transportation networks are critical infrastructure for post-earthquake emergency response, making proactive seismic risk assessment essential. However, existing frameworks often examine transportation components, interdependencies, and cascading effects separately, making it difficult to integrate them into a unified seismic-risk framework for transportation systems. This study introduces the Urban Transportation System Abstraction Hierarchy (UTSAH), a directed graph–based framework integrating abstraction hierarchy theory with network analysis across five hierarchical levels. Within this framework, UTSAH identifies dominant risk drivers and critical transmission chokepoints within a unified hierarchical structure, enabling simultaneous diagnosis of where risk originates and how it propagates. By determining weighted interdependencies among 131 transportation-specific parameters spanning physical, functional, social, governance, economic, and environmental dimensions, UTSAH provides a unified multi-dimensional assessment of seismic risk propagation and cascading effects in urban transportation networks. Based on graph-based analysis, interventions are classified into three strategic objectives: (i) mitigating cascading effects by seismic retrofitting of vulnerable bridges and tunnels and strengthening construction quality control and periodic inspections; (ii) preserving system connectivity by maintaining emergency transportation network continuity and enhancing route redundancy; and (iii) strengthening vulnerable high-level goals by improving accessibility to critical service centers such as hospitals and fire stations. Overall, UTSAH provides a system-oriented decision-support tool for identifying and classifying candidate seismic risk mitigation strategies in urban transportation networks.

business.title: A Generative AI-powered navigation system for precision CBCT-guided lung biopsies: a randomized controlled trial
business.desc: Lung puncture biopsy is the gold standard for the qualitative diagnosis of lung nodules. Cone Beam CT (CBCT) is commonly used for guiding punctures to locate lung nodules. However, the poor quality of CBCT images and the limited intelligence of surgical guidance systems have lowered the efficiency of puncture procedures, particularly for small and complex lesions. This study developed and validated a robust and accurate Generative AI-Powered Puncture Surgery Navigation System for lung punctures (GPS-Lung), demonstrating clinical applicability through a multicenter randomized controlled trial (Registration number: NCT06762613). The clinical results showed significant improvements in surgeon performance with the assistance of the integrated GPS-Lung system. Specifically, the system facilitated a more standardized and efficient operational process, reducing number of punctures (2.0 ± 1.2 vs. 2.5 ± 1.7, P = 0.005), shortening operative time (20.4 ± 5.6 min vs. 23.2 ± 6.3 min, P = 0.001), decreasing radiation exposure (4357.4 ± 3427.3 μGy·m2 vs. 5570.9 ± 4846.7 μGy·m2, P = 0.033), and reducing pneumothorax complications (12.7% vs. 23.9%, P = 0.033). Taken together, the proposed system demonstrates promising clinical and translational value in lung nodule puncture intervention. (Clinical Trials Registration: NCT06762613). Clinical Trials Registration: NCT06762613, Registration Date: March 26, 2025. (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06762613?term=NCT06762613&rank=1&tab=history).

business.title: Adaptive multi-scale YOLOv8s framework for defect detection in photovoltaic facilities
business.desc: Photovoltaic (PV) modules are widely used in building-integrated photovoltaic systems and renewable energy infrastructure. Accurate defect detection is essential for improving the reliability, energy efficiency, and sustainable operation of PV systems. However, existing deep learning-based inspection methods still suffer from missed detections, imprecise localisation of small defects, and limited robustness under complex operating conditions due to variations in defect scales and background interference. This study proposes an adaptive multi-scale attention-enhanced YOLOv8s framework (AMA-YOLOv8s) for intelligent PV module defect detection. Compared with the baseline YOLOv8s, the proposed framework incorporates three newly designed modules specifically developed for PV defect detection: the Adaptive Bottleneck Attention Mechanism (ABAM), Multi-scale Adaptive Fusion Module (MSAFM), and Adaptive Pooling Fusion Module (APFM). ABAM is introduced to enhance defect-related feature representation and suppress irrelevant background information, whereas MSAFM and APFM are designed to strengthen multi-scale feature fusion and improve the detection of small and irregular defects. In addition, a comprehensive PV defect dataset was constructed by integrating publicly available images, field-collected samples, and data augmentation strategies. Experimental results show that AMA-YOLOv8s achieves a precision of 93.2%, an F1-score of 92.7%, and an mAP@0.5 of 93.5% on the current evaluation dataset. Compared with the YOLOv8s baseline, the AMA-YOLOv8s provides incremental improvements in detection performance while maintaining a comparable real-time inference speed. Its overall performance is competitive with the evaluated detectors, although recent lightweight YOLO variants retain advantages in some individual metrics and computational complexity. These results demonstrate the practical effectiveness of the proposed coordinated attention and multi-scale feature-fusion design for PV defect detection.

technology.title: How Inversion and NASA Plan to Unlock Interplanetary Aerocapture MB edits
technology.desc: Using a planet’s atmosphere to secure a satellite’s place in orbit, a process known as “aerocapture”, has been the dream of flight engineers for decades. The only problem? It’s really hard to actually do. It requires control systems, thermal management, and orbital mechanics to all coordinate in a dance that allows a spacecraft to not just slow down while passing by another planet (or moon in some cases) but to start to orbit it without the use of lots of additional propellant. For now, that remains a dream, but a recent NASA contract to a California start-up called Inversion is another step towards making it a reality.
